Dundee manager wanted to ‘crawl under a rock and hide’ after 8-0 home thrashing

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Steven Pressley revealed the embarrassment of Dundee’s 8-0 hammering by Hearts on Saturday left him wanting to “crawl under a rock and hide”.
  • The Dark Blues manager has shouldered full responsibility after his team suffered their heaviest-ever home league defeat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Steven Pressley revealed the embarrassment of Dundee’s 8-0 hammering by Hearts on Saturday left him wanting to “crawl under a rock and hide”.

The Dark Blues manager has shouldered full responsibility after his team suffered their heaviest-ever home league defeat.

It has been revealed that speaking as Dundee prepared to return to action at Hibernian on Tuesday, Pressley stated: “It’s been a difficult 24-48 hours. There’s been a lot of hurt, a lot of embarrassment. As you can imagine, at times I’ve wanted to crawl under a rock and hide.

“It’s difficult on the back of such a disappointing result. But I will say this, I suffer a lot from vulnerability at times, but for some reason during difficult moments I seem to find strength from somewhere.

“I don’t know if it’s from my family, from messages that I’ve received, from my reading.

Industry observers note that “But I’ve had to show strength, I have to support the players. I have to make sure we navigate our way out of what was a really embarrassing moment.

“We had a good meeting yesterday. We chatted a lot about the various aspects, and hopefully we can start responding to the disappointment.”.

Pressley said he had feared a setback coming for Dundee – “not 8-0 but a disappointing performance” – because he had “sensed a little bit of subconscious complacency”.

The manager felt his team had been over-hyped by outsiders on the back of a start to the season in which they won five of their 12 matches before the international break.

“We’re nowhere near the levels that people keep telling us we are,” he stressed. “We’re not a good enough team not to do the hard yards. Our whole strength has been built on the cohesion of the team, the unity of the team, the aggressiveness of the team.

In a recent development, “And I think what Saturday did highlight is exactly what I’ve been saying. If we get lazy on the hard yards, we’re a very vulnerable team.

“We have to be at our absolute best to get results. If we fall below that, we’re nowhere near the levels that people have been telling us we’re at.”.

Pressley said Saturday has to represent “a reset moment, a moment we can always come back to to help us become better”. Asked if he expected a positive response from his players at Easter Road just 72 hours on from their Hearts humbling, he said: “I don’t know.

“I know that they’re hurting. I know that they want to respond in the best possible way. That part I don’t question. I know how much it’s affected them.

Industry observers note that “But we’ve not had a lot of time. I just hope we can bring some pride back to the football club with the right type of performance.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chloe Mustaki is a key figure for Carla Ward's Republic of Ireland side.
  • Republic of Ireland defender Chloe Mustaki has been forced to withdraw from her side's 2027 Women's World Cup play-off final against Poland next month after rupturing her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).
  • The 31-year-old sustained the injury in action for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool in the League Cup last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chloe Mustaki is a key figure for Carla Ward's Republic of Ireland side.

Republic of Ireland defender Chloe Mustaki has been forced to withdraw from her side's 2027 Women's World Cup play-off final against Poland next month after rupturing her anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

The 31-year-old sustained the injury in action for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool in the League Cup last week.

Her club have confirmed the centre-back will miss the rest of the season and that their medical team will "determine the best course of action for her rehabilitation and recovery".

Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward mentioned she was "absolutely devastated" for the player who will be a huge loss in the side's efforts to make it the tournament in Brazil next summer.

She added: "It is a huge blow for the entire squad because of how crucial she is to this group, both on the pitch with her consistency and leadership, and off the pitch with the incredible character and positivity she brings to the dressing room.

It has been revealed that "This is a really difficult setback, but Chloe is loved by us all. Everyone in the squad, the staff and the association is fully behind her, and we will give her all the love and support she needs to make a full recovery.".

Ward will not call up a replacement to her squad with the 24-player panel set to gather in Dublin on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that they will play the first leg of the play-off in Gdansk on 1 December with the return fixture at the Aviva Stadium four days later. Both games kick off at 17:00 GMT.

Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training.
  • Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on challenges that matter to them, such as climate protection.
  • What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on challenges that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today.".

Recent findings suggest that "Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," states Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests.".

It has been revealed that the 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

In a recent development, UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

In a recent development, this economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Recent findings suggest that nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30.".

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," indicates Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an key step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," claims Brod.

Recent findings suggest that sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!".

This article was originally published in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

Recent findings suggest that this would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

Industry observers note that that was a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, he can still bend the game to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

Industry observers note that this was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great banner on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

Afterwards, Kane made a point of thanking the Football Association for organising it all, although it was also clear that this was no less than he expected. “It’s important to recognise the great players,” he said, “and it’s not something we have always done over the years.”.

It has been revealed that if the sentiment was a little awkwardly articulated, he is certainly right on the key point: so many England careers have ended abruptly at tournament elimination or elsewhere. Yet here was one being celebrated with the man himself, in what might even be argued to be his prime. Kane, 33, was asked again as to how long he might continue and did not rule out going on to 40, “if I’m performing at the highest level”.

According to recent reports, that was a nod to Modric, a second-half substitute at the age of 41 and now on 207 caps for Croatia and almost 1,200 senior games. This Croatia team still seem unable to part company with their greatest player, despite his struggles against England in the seven-goal defeat in Rijeka. On this occasion, Croatia were much better.

It has been revealed that it should have been more straightforward for England. They had taken the lead through Morgan Rogers midway through the first half and had dominated the first hour. But Quansah’s mistake gave Croatia an equaliser, and after Kane’s penalty England were fortunate to survive on occasions.

“It was a tight match – a tough one,” Thomas Tuchel, the England manager, remarked. “We didn’t take our chances when we had chances, so it stayed a tight match. It cannot be glamorous and super-exciting [all the time]. It has to be serious and determined. We wanted a final on Sunday in Spain and we have that.”.

The win means that England’s game in Madrid on Sunday against Spain, who beat the Czech Republic and lead the Nations League group by three points, has some bite to it. Another England win would mean they would overtake Spain on goal difference and win the group ahead of the Nations League quarter-finals in March.

This was one game when the players might have wondered if they were due more from a Wembley crowd that went through the motions in the first half and scarcely returned for the second. For the first hour, England dominated a Croatia side who often invited six blue shirts into their back line. Tuchel mentioned his decision to select Dan Burn in the left-sided centre-half position over the left-footed Jarrad Branthwaite was almost split – a “51 per cent decision”.

England would break through just once, when Rogers got enough of his laces on an awkward Jude Bellingham cross deflected behind him and the shot brushed Josko Gvardiol on the way in.

Sources indicate that trent Alexander-Arnold started his third England game of the autumn and the right-back spent most of it in midfield. From the left it was his pass to Bellingham on the right wing that prefaced the cross for the Rogers goal.

The catastrophe of the defeat last month for Croatia meant they were naturally conservative. Nevertheless, in Martin Baturina, the 23-year-old Como attacking midfielder, they have another fine talent. When Modric did come on, he was applauded on all sides of Wembley. The home fans would later boo the arrival of Ben White, still not forgiven for his 2022 mid-tournament World Cup departure.

The equaliser was a Quansah error when the defender tried to head a loose corner back to Jordan Pickford and did not make the distance. Petar Sucic intervened and pushed it home with a right foot. Three minutes later it was judged a foul on Quansah by Ivan Smolcic when he pulled the Englishman down and the referee Krogh eventually gave the penalty.

Kane scored that and the substitute James Garner had a goal disallowed in the closing stages of the game, which were much less comfortable for England.

England manager Thomas Tuchel, speaking to ITV: “Good win. We wanted this win desperately and I think we deserved it. I think it was hard work against a good opponent. It took us a while to grow into the game but after 15 minutes I think we did OK, got the goal and got better and more confident and had some good actions and good chances, good half-chances.

“Got a little bit sloppy at the very end of the first half, started the second half very good, didn’t score the second goal, conceded from a set piece, and then showed a good reaction.

“We got the job done and it was important because it was a special occasion for Harry [Kane] and he scored the winner, so perfect evening.”.

On whether England were sloppy when they conceded: “It was maybe only three or four minutes before we gave passes away and especially in a moment when we were clearly the better team, we came with a very strong reaction after the half-time, had a beautiful chance created from Declan Rice and they blocked it on the line. It was like our third goal was coming and we had some easy ball losses in our own half that killed our momentum.

“An awkward moment in our box can always happen. It’s important to react and we did it.”.

According to recent reports, on his defenders: “Good. It was demanding for Dan Burn and also for Jarell [Quansah] because they [Croatia] play with a back five and have two number 10s in between the lines.

“It was a lot of work to do, a lot of communication but they did very well.”.

On what will be better against Spain on Sunday: “I don’t know. Everything will be different. Completely different scenario, completely different setup, but I’m very positive that we will get what we want.”.

England put in an the-Lord-Mayor’s-show performance following their 7-0 victory over Croatia. But it was still good enough to beat the same opponents 2-1 on the night Harry Kane celebrated his 126th record-breaking cap at Wembley.

Kane capped the night with the winning goal from the penalty spot, but a poor second-half showing – after Morgan Rogers had opened the scoring in the 24th minute – allowed Petar Sucic to equalise, aided by a dreadful mistake by Jarell Quansah.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Windsor Park would require 5,000 additional seats to host games at the 2035 World Cup.

The Irish Football Association's director of women's football Angela Platt said the organisation is "still working through" plans with the Northern Ireland government to ensure there is funding available to make the necessary upgrades to Windsor Park in time for the 2035 World Cup.

It was confirmed on Monday that Northern Ireland, England, Scotland and Wales, the only bidders for the tournament in nine years' time, had been ratified as co-hosts.

Of the 19 venues proposed by the 'All Together' bid, Belfast's Windsor Park is the sole stadium in Northern Ireland, but would require an additional 5,000 seats to its current capacity of 18,500 as well as changes to the pitch and floodlights.

"We're obviously working with our government partners who've committed their support to help us do that, and we'll continue our endeavours to make sure that we work towards that," Platt told BBC NI's Stephen Watson.

"We know that the Northern Ireland Executive has given a commitment to back us and do whatever they can to support us in our endeavours to make sure we're ready for that hosting of the Women's World Cup in 2035.

"We have a few years to make sure we work through that.".

Northern Ireland was involved in a similar bid to host games at Euro 2028, but aims for fixtures in Belfast at that tournament fell through when the government mentioned it would not provide funding to redevelop Casement Park in the required timescale.

Platt stated that "was in the past" and that the organisation were focused on the work required to avoid any repeat.

Recent findings suggest that "We're still working towards making sure that it does happen and we're positive. We know that the work is there to make sure that it happens," she added.

"It's obviously disappointing when something that people work so hard to put together doesn't come to fruition, but certainly that's in the past for us.

"From our perspective, working for women's football, this is a great opportunity for Northern Ireland to get behind this and actually make sure that we do everything we can to host our Women's World Cup games here.".

UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms.

Looks to increase Windsor Park capacity to 23,750.

There is no guarantee that, even as co-hosts, there would an automatic qualification spot for Northern Ireland.

The side last qualified for a major tournament at Euro 2022 and Platt believes bringing the World Cup to the country has the potential to "inspire a newly introduced generation".

Industry observers note that "I think it can have a huge impact. We've always been blessed that we have had our women's team involved in the Women's Euros in 2022, and through my role, I get to visit other nations hosting tournaments such as this," she said.

"I was in Sydney for the Women's World Cup (2023) and obviously saw the impact hosting a tournament like that had in Upcoming Zealand and Australia, and likewise for the Euros in England and Switzerland recently.

In a recent development, "That impact is significant. It's the growth of the game, it's the engagement, it's the legacy. So much positivity can come out of hosting major tournaments and we're excited to play our part in this and it can only have benefits for Northern Ireland in general.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beattie won the last of her 13 caps last year while the uncapped Haughey was last called into the senior squad in 2021.

Michael McArdle has decided the upcoming friendly double-header against Greece is the perfect time to bring back Kerry Beattie and Ella Haughey from the international wilderness.

Glentoran midfielder Chloe McCarron is also in under McArdle for the first time after a lengthily absence, but the Glentoran midfielder would likely have been included sooner if not for a spell on the sidelines through injury.

Beattie won her last cap a year ago while Haughey will hope to make a senior debut in one of the two games against Greece at Inver Park after she was an unused substitute in friendlies against England and Scotland in her sole call up in 2021.

The inclusion of both players, who have been in good form at their clubs, shows McArdle is willing to keep the door open for a return to the international squad if players are performing at club level.

Magill returns to NI squad for Greece friendlies.

Beattie has four goals in her 13 NI caps.

Portsmouth striker Beattie has been in and out of squads since her debut in 2021.

The 24-year-old has four goals in 13 caps, the last of which she won against Iceland in the Nations League play-off a year ago.

A prolific forward during two spells at Glentoran, she has struggled for consistency in moves across to Scotland with the likes of Glasgow City, Hearts and Aberdeen.

She left the Dons in the summer and consulted with McArdle when deciding upon her next move, before joining WSL 2 side Portsmouth.

Beattie has eight goals in all competitions for a Pompey side languishing at the bottom of the table and McArdle is pleased she has settled in well.

"Kerry had spells at Hearts and Aberdeen and for whatever reason it didn't quite work out at both, she had good spells but not a consistent run to express herself," McArdle noted.

"The move to Portsmouth, I was delighted she reached out to me for some advice, it's an alignment for her and it's been a great move on and off the pitch. It's allowed her to enjoy herself but also play 90 minutes and be that focal point striker.

"She will have been disappointed not to make the squad for the [World Cup] play-off [against Portugal] with her form but she worked hard and she's back in, I'm delighted for her.".

Beattie faces stiff competition for the starting striker role from the likes of returning captain Simone Magill and Kess Elmore, who impressed in the last camp and scored against Portugal, but she should receive some minutes across the two games and will be keen to grasp her chance to make an impact.

Left-back Haughey was called up to the senior squad as a 16-year-old under Kenny Shiels, but did not feature.

West Brom defender Haughey's last involvement with NI came when she represented the under-19s in 2023.

A Lisburn Rangers player when Kenny Shiels included her in the senior squad as a 16-year-old, Haughey then moved to Nottingham Forest before settling at the Baggies, who play in the National League.

The left-back, 22, has been a regular this season for the club in the third tier and combines playing with her university studies.

Left-back has been a problem position for NI which McArdle has been trying to address as demonstrated by him bringing in Lucy-Jayne Grant in the last camp and Haughey for this window to allow Rebecca Holloway to play as a central defender.

Haughey will be competing with Grant to fill that full-back role on the left side and McArdle believes she is more than capable of doing so having tried to bring her back into the squad earlier in his reign.

Sources indicate that "Ella's been at West Brom for a few years now. She has real potential, strong, athletic potential. We tried to call her up sooner but there were some challenges," he explained.

It has been revealed that "She's probably been one of their top performers and one of the top performers in the league. Delighted she's earned this opportunity and hopefully she can make her debut and achieve her first cap.".

McArdle has made a concerted to continue to widen the player pool available to him as he aims to build depth ahead of the Nations League campaign next year, but if Beattie and Haughey catch the eye it will show that giving chances to those previously involved under different managers could be another possibility.

Why is Kai Havertz always offside for Arsenal this season?

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that injuries hardly aided Kai Havertz last season.
  • In a recent development, in the Champions League final showdown with Paris Saint-Germain, Arteta again called on the German, and was duly rewarded as he fired the north London side in front with just six minutes on the clock.
  • Sources indicate that saying that, there is more to Havertz’s game than just putting the ball in the back of the net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that injuries hardly aided Kai Havertz last season. Regardless, his standing within the Arsenal squad was evidently high. As the Gunners went in search of a first Premier League title for 22 years, he was the one who Mikel Arteta turned to during the run-in, despite Viktor Gyokeres’ substantial money summer arrival from Sporting CP.

In a recent development, in the Champions League final showdown with Paris Saint-Germain, Arteta again called on the German, and was duly rewarded as he fired the north London side in front with just six minutes on the clock. Unsurprisingly, Havertz remains the Gunners’ first-choice frontman, even if a return of three goals in the opening 10 league outings is hardly a great return.

Sources indicate that saying that, there is more to Havertz’s game than just putting the ball in the back of the net. The Germany international’s selflessness and impressive link-up play is a key reason behind his continued selection ahead of a more natural No. 9 in Gyokeres. Arteta wants his leading forward to drop deeper to bring teammates into play, dragging markers out of position to open up space for the wingers to exploit.

Recent findings suggest that and yet, his offside numbers resemble that of former AC Milan and Italy icon Filippo Inzaghi. “That lad must have been born offside,” Sir Alex Ferguson once quipped about the Italian, who addressed the comments to FourFourTwo back in 2023. In the modern day, Ferguson’s quote would be applicable to Havertz.

In a recent development, after all, Havertz has been flagged offside 15 times in the Premier League this season. It’s almost double that of the player in second for this metric, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin (8) his closest competitor. He’s been penalised for being in the wrong place more times than four Premier League teams.

For context, Bukayo Saka was caught offside more times (14) than any other player in the 2025/26 Premier League campaign. Havertz did so on just three occasions. “Certainly, it’s far too many,” Arteta said of the number of times Arsenal have been caught offside in the Premier League this season following the 1-0 win over Hull City prior to the international break.

So, for a player who is renowned for dropping deep in order to help his side in the final third, why has Kai Havertz been flagged offside so often this season?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Well, for a start, Arsenal are a team that see more of the ball than the majority of the other 19 teams in England’s top tier. Only Manchester City (65.9%) and Tottenham Hotspur (63%) have managed a greater possession share than the defending champions (59.8%) in the Premier League. A return of 1379 successful final third passes is the second-most. So, too, is 31 total through balls.

Recent findings suggest that it’s only natural that the amount of final third passes would result in a higher number of offsides. When teams attack an opposition backline, the side on the back foot will understandably work harder to catch you offside.

Who is to blame then? Obviously Havertz is at fault but he’s making the requisite runs to try and get in on goal.

According to Opta, only Fulham’s Gonzalo Garcia (145) and Manchester United forward Bryan Mbeumo (141) have made more in-behind high-intensity runs than Havertz (125) in the Premier League this season.

Despite his gangly appearance, the former Chelsea man is deceptively quick off the mark.

According to recent reports, he’s playing off the shoulder of the last defender, and if those in support were prepared to release the ball a little quicker, then his runs would be capitalised upon to great effect. However, his teammates have been guilty of taking an extra touch, or taking a split-second longer to play the pass for Havertz. As such, his momentum takes him beyond the last man, meaning he either needs to check his run late, and a chance breaks down, or stray offside.

Of course, as things stand, Arsenal are hardly faltering domestically as a result of Havertz’s fondness for the flag. Admittedly, though, 15 goals scored doesn’t make for great reading - it’s level with Ipswich Town. And there will come a moment where these ill-timed runs and passes do have a detrimental impact on the team. “Yes, it’s something to improve,” Arteta added following the Hull triumph. It’s an issue that he concedes requires focus.

Yet Arsenal’s relentlessness combined with a watertight backline that has shipped just five goals means they are managing to get the job done.

Recent findings suggest that six of their 10 league wins have been by a single goal. A little more synchronisation between Havertz and the ammo suppliers would go a long way to give Arsenal more breathing space in their title defence.

The home nations expect Fifa to be in a “different place” by the time they host the Women’s World Cup in 2035 after withdrawing their support for president Gianni Infantino earlier this year.

The joint bid from England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales was approved at the Fifa Congress on Monday, although it was the sole bidder to host the 48-team tournament and was voted through by acclamation.

The tournament will be the first World Cup to be held in the UK since England hosted the men’s World Cup in 1966, but it comes just months after the chair of the English FA, Debbie Hewitt, demanded an independent investigation into Infantino’s scrapped World Cup sell-off plan and the Folarin Balogun affair, as well calls for further Fifa reform.

Infantino has retained the support required for re-election in March but cannot continue beyond 2031, and the FA’s director of women’s football Sue Day believes there will be significant change within Fifa as the home nations prepare to work alongside the governing body on staging the World Cup in 2035.

There have already been some challenges, with Fifa reportedly demanding tax-free status from ticket sales and broadcast and commercial partnerships, something that the UK government has not allowed when previously hosting major events such as the 2012 Olympics and will not offer to Uefa when they stage Euro 2028.

“There are two separate complications here, the concerns around the Fifa leadership and their proposals, and then this World Cup,” Day remarked on Monday.

“We very much want today to be about the excitement of this World Cup and we didn't want those concerns to get in the way of us trying to land the opportunity to put on this amazing tournament that we think can change the world of football.

“By the time the tournament comes around, lots of things will have changed. We expect Fifa to be in a different place.

“We know that there is a brilliant team there right now, led by Jill Ellis [former USA manager, now Fifa’s Chief Football Officer], leading women’s football and we're really looking forward to working with them on developing the tournament.”.

Sources indicate that day also said that the home nations hope to have a “strong influence” on the pricing of the tournament. Fifa were accused of “betrayal” and price gouging when the ticket prices were revealed for last summer’s men’s World Cup in North American last summer but tickets for the 2027 Women’s World Cup in Brazil will go on sale for as little as £4 next month.

But Fifa is targeting revenues of $4bn when it stages the first 48-team World Cup in 2031, in the United States, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, and will be setting similar targets for the England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales bid.

Sources indicate that “At the moment, the model is absolutely that Fifa decides those things,” Day noted. “We will hope to be able to have a really strong influence on some of that because we know our audiences best.

“It’s going to be really notable to get the pricing right. We all know that we need to show the commercial viability of women’s football, and we want this to be an accessible tournament.”.

A 48-team Women’s World Cup would see the UK will host 104 matches across 39 days in 2035, in the largest single-sport event ever to be staged in the country, and Day stated success for the tournament will be judged on its potential to transform society as well as what happens on the pitch.

Sources indicate that “This is genuinely once in a lifetime, once in a generation,” Day remarked. “There wouldn’t have been a World Cup on this soil since 1966, which would be nearly 70 years away.

“And so I think just collectively, I want us to grasp the opportunity of this moment and really build towards it and think of it as, it will be the most amazing tournament, but it's [also] a catalyst for growth and inspiration and something to springboard from.

“I think we can change the world a little bit with the tournament and we should aim that high. Why wouldn't we aim that high?”.

#174140. Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most key temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
  • Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
  • It has been revealed that the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most key temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

It has been revealed that the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

It has been revealed that the east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Sources indicate that brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle.".

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

It has been revealed that in 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

According to recent reports, then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!".

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go.".

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another key discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most key fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

Industry observers note that there is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

#174138. John Toshack on Bill Shankly, Liverpool and an extraordinary football career

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2938 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fourfourtwo ↗ Open Full Page

John Toshack on Bill Shankly, Liverpool and an extraordinary football career

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bill Shankly knew how to make an instant impact on players.
  • It has been revealed that the Welshman has never forgotten Shankly’s first words to him.
  • Recent findings suggest that over the next eight years, Toshack’s religious experience would develop him from a highly promising forward into an Anfield legend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bill Shankly knew how to make an instant impact on players. The year was 1970 and John Toshack had just joined Liverpool from Cardiff for a club-record £110,000 fee, when he was greeted by his new manager.

It has been revealed that the Welshman has never forgotten Shankly’s first words to him. “I was only 21 and didn’t have a driving licence, so I travelled from Cardiff by train,” Toshack recounts to FourFourTwo. “Bill Shankly was waiting for me at the station, with his trilby on his head. The first thing he remarked to me was, ‘Welcome to Liverpool, son: you’ve come out of school to come to church’.”.

Recent findings suggest that over the next eight years, Toshack’s religious experience would develop him from a highly promising forward into an Anfield legend. That day at Liverpool Lime Street station, his extraordinary life in football was just getting started.

Today, 55 years later, following a career that took him to a dozen countries, he lives in Besalu – a village of medieval architecture in Catalonia, not far from the French border – with his wife, Mai, and several dogs they’ve adopted. As a manager, Toshack had seven spells in Spain: three at Real Sociedad, two with Real Madrid, plus stints at Deportivo La Coruna and Real Murcia. He welcomes FFT into his rural home, telling us he used to read the magazine when he lived in the UK.

Sources indicate that time hasn’t eroded a single detail of his extensive career, right back to his school days in his home city of Cardiff. “I’d take my sandwich with me so I didn’t have to go home for lunch – it meant I could stay and play football in the playground,” explains Toshack with a smile. Not just football, either: “I played cricket during the week, rugby on Saturday mornings and football in the afternoon,” he adds.

Then the first scouts appeared. At 15, he received an offer from Tottenham to go to London for trials. “I went with two other team-mates to a residence next to the old White Hart Lane,” he recalls. “We trained, and I thought they were going to give me a chance. But when I returned home, I got a letter thanking me but saying they didn’t believe I was good enough. I was gutted.”.

His father, George, was a carpenter; a self-made man from Scotland. Young John’s mother encouraged him not to drop out of school, wanting him to have an alternative if he didn’t achieve his ultimate goal of becoming a footballer. Toshack, however, soon began breaking barriers locally. His first-team debut for Cardiff came aged 16, against Leyton Orient. Back then, only one substitution was allowed per team. “I came on with 10 minutes to go and scored a goal,” he claims. “I can still visualise it today, if I close my eyes. A week later, we travelled up north to Middlesbrough. I started and scored two goals in 20 minutes. We won 4-3. It was a dream start.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Industry observers note that making a name for himself in the Second Division, Toshack caught the eye of Fulham in 1968. “Bobby Robson came in with an offer of £60,000, which was good money at the time,” he states. “But I thought London was too massive for a boy from South Wales, and turned it down. The Cardiff management were outraged at my decision. The transfer would have been a big money-spinner for them.”.

According to recent reports, toshack would score exactly 100 goals for Cardiff, in 207 appearances. More approaches were inevitable. In 1970, one arrived from Liverpool, who were attempting to return to the summit of English football after title triumphs under Shankly in 1964 and 1966. Cardiff boss Jimmy Scoular lived down the road from Toshack, and delivered the news. “I saw him one Sunday morning and I knew he wanted to tell me something key,” continues Toshack. “He had read the papers, and they said Liverpool were coming for me. Shankly had offered £110,000, which was a record amount. Jimmy told me that we couldn’t say no. I thought, ‘This time, I’m ready’. Besides, Liverpool wasn’t Fulham.”.

Anfield awaited. “There was a lot of expectation,” admits Toshack. “In those days, we barely warmed up – we’d come out five minutes before kick-off and you could hear You’ll Never Walk Alone. The noise was deafening.”.

Industry observers note that his debut was rushed: he had suffered a minor ankle injury in his last game for Cardiff, but media expectation and his own desire to pull on a Liverpool shirt won out. “The following week, after treatment, it was the Merseyside derby against Everton,” he notes. “It couldn’t have been better. There were 54,000 supporters in the stands, 27,000 of them behind the Kop, all on their feet. I scored my first goal with a header from Steve Heighway’s cross, against Everton’s centre-back, Brian Labone. That’s when my love story with Liverpool began.”.

According to recent reports, playing at Anfield never ceased to be a thrill. “We liked to attack the goal at the Kop end in the second half, in front of all of those fans, but other clubs knew that and tried to win the toss to spite us,” says Toshack, chuckling. Not long after the 6ft 1in striker’s arrival, a fellow young forward called Kevin Keegan signed from Scunthorpe United. A famous partnership was born.

Sources indicate that “Shankly put us together in attack in training, and there was great chemistry between the two of us from the start,” says Toshack. “Keegan would say to me, ‘Anywhere you like, Tosh’. I’d jump up with a smile on my face, as I knew that if I won the jump and touched the ball, he’d find it for a finish.

“We understood each other so well that we were once invited onto a TV show to see if telepathy existed between us. They put our backs to each other and we had to guess the colour or the number of a paddle that the other one held up. I saw them reflected in the camera. I got them all right and he got none. He was scared! I noted to him, ‘You see which of us is the clever one: you run but I’m the one who gets it right here!’”.

The duo would combine for six years, thanks to Shankly’s decision to pair them up. “I owe almost everything to Shankly and to Liverpool,” says Toshack. “He was basic, direct and uncomplicated in his message. He was sharp, provocative and liked to pick on Everton. He’d say, ‘Everton play so bad that if they played in my garden, I would draw the curtains so I couldn’t see them’.”.

Industry observers note that in 1973, Shankly’s Liverpool won the league and the UEFA Cup, the club’s first European silverware. After the final, the manager asked his players to come to his office to renew their contracts, one by one. “I noted to him, ‘Boss, I’ve been top scorer; I’m on £80,000 and I think £90,000 would be good’,” Toshack tells FFT. “He said, ‘Ninety? No. You deserve £100,000’. I left his office excited, but before I got to the car, I thought, ‘He’s cheated me – he was going to give me more’. Years later, I spoke to him and he admitted it: he was going to give me £120,000! That was Shankly.”.

In a recent development, shankly’s assistant, Bob Paisley, took over when he retired a year later. “They were the perfect blend,” claims Toshack. “But I always got the feeling that Paisley wasn’t a substantial fan of mine. He tried to sell me to Leicester in 1974, but as well as being a coach, he was a physiotherapist, and he could see that I was beginning to get muscle calcification. That’s what thwarted my departure.”.

In a recent development, still with years on his contract, but weakened by physical concerns, Toshack modified his game, becoming more selective about when to expend energy. “I knew that Keegan was much better alongside me – without me, he wouldn’t score so many goals – so I learned to think more,” he says. “Those were my first steps as a coach.”.

It has been revealed that two more league crowns followed at Anfield, although Toshack missed out on Liverpool’s victorious 1977 European Cup Final due to injury. Less than a year later, having plundered 96 goals for the club, he negotiated his release to move into coaching at the age of 28. That coaching career could have begun back at his old club, Cardiff, had manager Jimmy Andrews not rejected his initial enquiries, saying he wasn’t sufficiently qualified to join the club’s backroom staff. Instead, Toshack spoke to Cardiff’s rivals, Swansea, and was soon appointed player-manager of the Fourth Division club. He became the Football League’s youngest manager.

What ensued was quite remarkable: ascension to the third tier within two months, then another promotion a year later, courtesy of a goal from their boss on the last day of the season. “I was a substitute: number 12 on the bench,” he remembers. “The ground was full – 22,000 spectators – and we had to beat Chesterfield to go up. We went 1-0 down, then we were drawing, and I knew I couldn’t feature for more than 30 minutes. I had my assistant on the bench giving me the elbow, saying, ‘Hey, something has to be done...’ With 15 minutes to go, without warming up or anything, I said, ‘Come on, I’m going on’. Three minutes later: a cross from the left wing, I jumped and... goal!”.

Industry observers note that incredibly, Toshack led Swansea into the top flight two seasons later. Sealing promotion away at Preston meant that in the three years and 62 days after his appointment, Toshack – still only 32 years of age – had taken the Swans from the Fourth Division to the First Division.

Industry observers note that “We had to win – no other result would do,” he tells us. “I invited Shankly, who had played more than 300 matches for Preston. He gave a talk to my players in the hotel and they listened attentively; he was almost a god-like figure. Some 15,000 Swansea fans came all the way from Wales, and we did it. Nobby Stiles, Preston’s manager, very graciously came over to congratulate me.”.

In a recent development, the rise continued. Swansea – in their first ever top-flight season, barely seven years on from needing re-election to the Football League – led the First Division as late as the final week of March, before eventually finishing sixth. In an early 2-2 draw at Anfield, an already-significant fixture for the ex-Liverpool man became particularly poignant when Shankly died in the week of the match. “The day before the game, I carried his coffin with three other team-mates,” says Toshack. “I was in shock – totally speechless. I wore a Swansea tracksuit during the game, but with a Liverpool shirt underneath.”.

His dream, of course, was to manage the Reds one day. “I was close – very close,” he claims. “I went to Liverpool and Paisley told me that he had to stay for another year because of his pension. I’d already spoken to secretary Peter Robinson and chairman John Smith in a private room in a hotel in Southport.

Recent findings suggest that “I’d told the Swansea chairman it was my last season. I thought it was done. But Liverpool went for Joe Fagan and I had to go back to Swansea. From then on, nothing worked out and Swansea were relegated. I lost my motivation.”.

Toshack needed a reset. After a year at Sporting in Portugal, he found happiness in Spain (“It’s been many years,” he claims now, but I feel so loved and recognised here”). He won the Copa del Rey in the first of three spells with Real Sociedad, then switched to Real Madrid in 1989. “It was a difficult start, as we lost to Barcelona at the Camp Nou, then were knocked out of the European Cup by Milan,” he reflects. “We lost 2-0 at San Siro, then won 1-0 at the Bernabeu. It was one of the greatest games of my coaching career. We couldn’t go crazy – we had to get back into the tie little by little – but to beat that team, with Frank Rijkaard, Marco van Basten and Ruud Gullit, was almost impossible.”.

Recent findings suggest that real Madrid won La Liga in Toshack’s first season, scoring a then-record 107 goals. “There were some critics who noted we were too defensive…” he laughs. Things didn’t go as well in his second spell, 10 years later. Arriving in February 1999, he took Los Blancos from sixth to a second-placed finish, but they were eighth early in the subsequent campaign when Toshack publicly slated goalkeeper Albano Bizzarri after a defeat to Rayo Vallecano. Asked by president Lorenzo Sanz to retract his comments, Toshack refused, chirping, “There’s more chance of a pig flying over the Bernabeu.” He was soon sacked.

According to recent reports, “That sentence will stay with me for life – just like the one about the usual 11 bastards, which was Shankly’s,” he says. “Shankly mentioned, ‘John, don’t think about picking the team for the next game on a Saturday night after losing, because you’re going to leave everyone out. On Sunday, ‘these two... they’re not bad’. When Wednesday comes, you prepare the team with the same 11 bastards as last week’.”.

It has been revealed that toshack’s face lights up when recalling his experience managing Wales from 2004 to 2010. He’d briefly led his nation in 1994, combining the job with his role at Real Sociedad, but resigned after 47 days. When he returned a decade later, replacing Mark Hughes, wins weren’t forthcoming but he believes he laid the foundations for future generations. “From day one,” indicates Toshack, “I made it very clear to the FAW that we may not qualify for the World Cup in Germany or the Euros in Austria and Switzerland, but with the under-21 coach, Brian Flynn, we were starting to give opportunities to youngsters like Aaron Ramsey, Joe Allen, Sam Vokes and, of course, Gareth Bale. Gareth was the chosen one.”.

Industry observers note that by then, Toshack had also managed in France with Saint-Etienne and in Italy with Catania. He headed to even more unexpected locations in the final years of his coaching career. He spent a year as manager of Macedonia (now North Macedonia), only for the relationship to break down because he didn’t want to live in the country; then came Khazar Lankaran in Azerbaijan. “It’s nice to feel the respect they have for you in more remote places,” he indicates. “My time there was short-lived, but I’m very fond of it.”.

According to recent reports, he also cherishes his two years in the Moroccan city of Casablanca, at the helm of Wydad. “We filled the stadium with 70,000 fans an hour before a match against Raja,” he says of the derby with Wydad’s city adversaries. “There are few places where I’ve experienced hotter atmospheres. We won the league title in 2015 but the following season, in the semi-final of the African Champions League, I was sacked.” Facing Zamalek in the first leg in Egypt, Wydad trailed 2-0 at the interval. “At half-time, I knew I was out – the doctor told me,” he says. “Our first and second goalkeepers were doing military service and the Moroccan government didn’t give them permission to play.” Wydad lost 4-0.

In 2018, Toshack signed a three-year deal with Tractor in Iran, but lasted only three months. “Someone reported me and my assistant for wearing shorts out in the street,” he lamented. “We were summoned to a police station. When we got there, all of the policemen were waving at us and asking for photos. As we climbed up the stairs, though, the atmosphere became more tense, until we reached the top, to the office of the captain. He greeted us loudly and rudely because wearing shorts is associated with homosexuality.”.

Industry observers note that the players were easier to manage. “We didn’t have to give out a single fine,” he says. “If the training session was at 10am, the kids were sitting and waiting at 9.30. They were very orderly.”.

Sources indicate that toshack hasn’t returned to football since. In February 2022, he spent nine days on life support inside a Barcelona hospital, suffering from a severe case of pneumonia caused by COVID. “I don’t remember much of that,” the 75-year-old tells FFT now. For his wife, however, it was terrifying experience. “John was dead,” explains Mai. “We were going on holiday to Majorca, but before we left home he just collapsed. We called for an ambulance and he was rushed off to hospital. They told us he was short of oxygen and that he’d also punctured a lung.

“Emilio Butragueno, a great friend of the family, called us every day.” Butragueno, once Toshack’s star striker at Real Madrid, sent a physical trainer to assist the Welshman in his recovery. “It was slow, but here we are,” notes Mai.

“Here we are – the same bastards as always,” adds her husband. Bill Shankly taught him well.

Jack Grealish has returned to the Everton squad for the first time since being dropped for a breach of discipline.

Grealish last played in a 2-0 home defeat to Chelsea on 17 October, with the former England international punished for skipping training when he was not authorised to do so before the Carabao Cup tie with Newcastle.

He has not featured in four games - the first of which, against Arsenal, due to illness - with manager David Moyes not including him in previous matchday squads due to a lack of match fitness.

But after featuring in a behind-closed-doors friendly against Derby during the international break, Grealish has returned to the first-team fold and starts on the bench for Everton’s trip to Brentford on Monday night.

Moyes has preferred Merlin Rohl, Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and Tyrique George in the attacking midfield positions behind Thierno Barry, but Grealish could be in line for a substitute cameo.

Grealish apologised to fans after his friendly return to action, writing on his Instagram story: "Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training.

"I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.

Sources indicate that "I love playing for this club and can’t wait to be back playing in front of you guys in an Everton shirt. See you all soon.".

Grealish spent the 2025-26 season on loan at Everton before injury disrupted his spell, but he secured another temporary deal on transfer deadline day.

In his absence, Everton have won three of their last four matches to move up to sixth in the Premier League table, while also earning their spot in the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Caroline Weir says it is "amazing" that Scotland will host the World Cup finals.

Scotland captain Caroline Weir says hosting the 2035 Women's World Cup along with England, Northern Ireland and Wales will usher in "an amazing decade of excitement" for the game in her homeland.

World governing body Fifa confirmed on Monday that the United Kingdom will host a football World Cup for the first time since England won the men's tournament on home soil in 1966.

Scotland's national stadium at Hampden Park in Glasgow and Hibernian's Easter Road Stadium in Leith are among 19 venues chosen for the 39-day competition involving 48 teams.

At the age of 31 now, Weir would have to show unusual longevity to still be playing at that point, but she still considers it "amazing news, not just for young players that hope to play there but for us, in this period in between, to develop the women's game in Scotland - and to push it.

"So I think it's amazing news and I think it's going to be an amazing decade of excitement leading into this World Cup".

Andreatta's masterplan to shock Sweden & take Scots to World Cup.

Substantial wins as Celtic, Rangers, City & Hearts progress.

The Lyon midfielder has already played for Scotland the only time they have so far qualified for a World Cup finals - in 2019.

"As a young, aspiring footballer watching football on TV growing up, for your home country to actually host a tournament itself, and the World Cup itself, the biggest tournament in football, is the most amazing thing," Weir stated.

"So, if I was a 10 or 11 year old girl now, I would be thinking this is the best news ever and I'm going to work and practice and hope that, one day, I am representing Scotland in a home nations tournament playing at Hampden Park in a World Cup for Scotland.

"I don't think it gets any bigger or better than that.".

Angie Hind, Scotland Under-23 head coach and Scottish FA player pathway manager, also thinks it will prove inspirational to the young players under her charge.

"If you think of the young players who are involved in our pathway right now, from 13 years old right through the 23s that I take, that's the future," the former Scotland midfielder told BBC Scotland.

"That's very much those players who will be pulling on a Scotland jersey when we are part of that World Cup.".

Hind pointed out that it "fits perfectly" with Project 2035, revealed this month by SFA and Scottish government, designed to boost the long-term growth of the girls and women's game.

For SFA head of women's and girls football Shirley Martin, it is a "tremendous milestone" considering holding a World Cup had been such "a game changer" for previous hosts.

It has been revealed that "Ten years ago, a home World Cup have felt like a dream and now it's happening," she told BBC Radio 5 live. "I think it highlights how far women's football has come.".

Martin pointed out that the SFA hopes to "double our participation over that time" as well as improving coaching, referees, clubs and facilities - and are already doing so.

However, she admitted: "The one thing we need to do is increase the crowds that come to matches.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Scottish FA president George Peat has died at the age of 86.

The former Airdrieonians and Stenhousemuir director spent four years in the role, taking over from John McBeth in 2007.

He oversaw the appointments of Scotland managers George Burley and Craig Levein and commissioned former first minister Henry McLeish to conduct a review of Scottish football.

Peat was also at the helm when Scottish referees opted to take strike action in November 2010.

"George loved his football and was renowned as a forthright personality and formidable negotiator but behind that imposing exterior lay a sharp wit and a glint in his eye," said current SFA president Mike Mulraney.

"He cared deeply about the national game and his beloved Airdrieonians.

"George was also passionate about the modernisation of the association and commissioned the McLeish Review of Scottish football as one of his first acts as president.

"He was a regular visitor to Hampden, even as his health deteriorated, and will be sadly missed by his friends and former colleagues at the Scottish FA and across the game.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.
  • But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.
  • "We are extremely concerned about the situation," remarked a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," remarked a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

Industry observers note that the IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this problem, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions.".

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action aims for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," mentioned a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Recent findings suggest that disagreements over budget complications have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," stated a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

Sources indicate that "We have no time to lose," mentioned an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive.".

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake.".

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra remarked it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science.".

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

In a recent development, the IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the plans to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment.".

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

Controversial refereeing decisions have been a part of football for a long as the game has been around, but one of the most bizarre incidents in recent memory occurred during Arsenal’s infamous 6-0 defeat to Chelsea in March 2014.

After spotting an Arsenal handball on the goal line, referee Andrer Marriner reached for his pocket and flashed a red card to Kieran Gibbs.

However, the glitch here was that it was actually Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain who had handled the ball, and in this pre-VAR era, Gibbs was forced into an early bath, despite the protests of players from both sides.

As Gibbs looks back on the incident more than a decade on, he remembers the confusion, the frustration and the surreal nature of the incident which wouldn’t be allowed to happen these days.

In a recent development, “It feels like a blur now, and it did at the time too,” he reflects to FourFourTwo. “It’s heated in the moment and you’re trying to focus on the game.”.

The incident came during a calamitous first half for the Gunners, who found themselves 2-0 down after just seven minutes in what was Arsene Wenger’s 1,000th game in charge of the club.

According to recent reports, the handball incident came in the 17th minute, when Oxlade-Chamberlain threw his left hand at an Eden Hazard shot, tipping it around the post. Marriner pointed to the spot and the referee was not for turning, despite widespread protests from both sets of players.

The Belgian would slot home the penalty to effectively end the game as a contest, with Gibbs still finding it remarkable that such an incident would occur, given the technology now used in the game.

“It feels crazy that there was no VAR, because you don’t have those kinds of complications anymore,” he continues.

“It was a surreal and very frustrating moment that was unique in the Premier League, so it brought a lot of attention.

“Both captains and the referee were telling me I was definitely going off.

“After a few minutes of protesting, I needed to listen to them.

“It was a big error from the referee, who apologised later and the red card was rescinded.”.

The return of Kevin De Bruyne represents Man City’s greatest joy and a major fear
